lesson.title: When the Tug of War Has a Winner
lesson.summary: A polar molecule is one whose bond dipoles do not cancel, leaving a permanent, measurable separation of partial positive and partial negative charge across the molecule.
lesson.body:
A polar molecule is the outcome you get when the vector summing process from molecular polarity does not end in a tie. Instead of the bond dipoles canceling, some net dipole moment survives, meaning the molecule has a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end even though it carries no overall electrical charge. Chemists mark these partial charges with the lowercase Greek delta symbol, writing delta plus on the electron poor end and delta minus on the electron rich end, to distinguish them clearly from the full charges on ions.

Water is the textbook polar molecule, and it is worth returning to because its polarity explains so much of its behavior. The bent shape means the two O-H bond dipoles point generally away from each other but not directly opposite, so their vector sum is nonzero and points from the hydrogen side toward the oxygen. The oxygen end of the molecule carries a partial negative charge, and the hydrogen end carries a partial positive charge. Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is a simpler example: it has just one bond, so there is no cancellation to worry about, and the bond dipole is the molecular dipole outright, with chlorine as the negative end and hydrogen as the positive end.

Polarity does not require an obviously lopsided shape. Ammonia, NH3, is trigonal pyramidal because nitrogen has one lone pair pushing the three N-H bonds into a pyramid rather than a flat triangle. The three N-H bond dipoles do not cancel with each other, and the lone pair itself contributes additional electron density on one side of the molecule, so ammonia has a clear net dipole pointing from the hydrogens toward the nitrogen and its lone pair. This shows that even a molecule with several identical bonded atoms can be polar if its geometry, often because of a lone pair, is not symmetric enough to force cancellation. Sulfur dioxide, SO2, makes the same point from a different angle: its bent shape, again the result of a lone pair on the central atom, prevents the two S=O bond dipoles from lining up opposite each other, so SO2 carries a net dipole even though a naive glance at its formula might suggest otherwise.

The practical consequence of being polar is that these molecules interact strongly with other polar molecules and with electric fields, because their permanent charge separation lets neighboring molecules line up positive to negative. This is the root of the phrase "like dissolves like": polar solvents such as water dissolve polar or ionic solutes well because the partial charges on the solvent can surround and stabilize the charges on the solute. Polar molecules also tend to have higher boiling points than nonpolar molecules of similar mass, a pattern explored in depth once dipole-dipole forces and hydrogen bonding are introduced later in this chapter. For now, the key identifying test is straightforward: draw the geometry, sum the bond dipoles, and if a net arrow survives, the molecule is polar.
